hook: A launch site is forming ninety miles from your coast.
short_setup: Public pressure favors force. The cost of misreading the other side could be nuclear war.
why_option_a_made_sense: An air strike offered speed and visible resolve. It might destroy the missile sites before more launchers became operational, reassure allies, and remove a direct strategic threat without waiting for Soviet cooperation. Senior military advisers could reasonably argue that delay allowed the danger to harden. Yet the information available at T0 did not guarantee that every missile and warhead would be found or destroyed, so the apparent decisiveness carried a serious risk of incomplete success followed by invasion and escalation.
why_option_b_made_sense: A naval quarantine was slower and did not remove missiles already in Cuba, but it created time, made the next escalation step reversible, and forced Soviet leaders to choose whether to challenge a clearly announced line. It also preserved air strikes and invasion as later options. The tradeoff was real: construction at the missile sites continued while diplomacy unfolded, and a confrontation at sea could itself ignite combat.
outcome_story: Kennedy announced the quarantine and demanded removal of the missiles. Soviet ships approaching the line slowed or turned, while construction in Cuba continued and both governments exchanged public and private messages. On October 28, Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles under verification in exchange for a public U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba. Separately and privately, Robert Kennedy indicated that obsolete U.S. Jupiter missiles in Turkey would be removed, though not as a public quid pro quo. The quarantine ended after further verification and removal of Soviet bombers.
hindsight_analysis: A slower action can be decisive when it preserves communication and limits irreversible escalation. The good outcome does not prove that quarantine was a guaranteed solution, nor does it make every advocate of an air strike irrational. At T0, the quarantine left missiles in place and gave the Soviet Union time to react. Its decision quality rests instead on sequencing: it demonstrated resolve, bought information, and preserved stronger actions if diplomacy failed. Later evidence makes the avoided downside even larger than Kennedy's team knew. U.S. intelligence had not located all Soviet nuclear warheads in Cuba, including weapons that could have been used against an invasion force. That unknown improves our understanding of the stakes; it must not be smuggled backward into the player's choice.
decision_principle: Under extreme stakes, prefer moves that preserve the next move.
longform_story:
On the morning of October 16, 1962, President John F. Kennedy learned that U.S. reconnaissance photographs showed Soviet offensive missile sites under construction in Cuba. The discovery created a compressed decision problem. If the missiles became operational, they would alter the strategic and political position of the United States. If Washington attacked, it could begin a war whose boundaries no one controlled.

The most direct option was an air strike against the missile sites, possibly followed by an invasion. Speed mattered. Every day could bring more construction, dispersal, and readiness. An air strike would show that secret deployment close to the United States could not stand. But the available intelligence could not guarantee destruction of every missile. Kennedy also objected to the political and moral character of a surprise attack. The official minutes record his concern that it would resemble Pearl Harbor and might still end in invasion.

The alternative that rose during ExComm deliberations was a naval quarantine. The label mattered because a blockade was traditionally an act of war. U.S. forces would stop further offensive military shipments while Kennedy publicly demanded withdrawal of the missiles already in Cuba. This did not solve the physical problem immediately. It deliberately exchanged speed for time and control. It also created a visible decision point for Soviet ships and left stronger military options available.

Kennedy selected the quarantine. On October 22 he announced the missiles to the public; on October 23 he signed the proclamation that authorized the naval action. The following days did not follow a clean script. Some Soviet ships stopped or turned, one tanker continued, missile-site work accelerated, and messages from Moscow shifted in tone and terms. A U.S. U-2 was shot down over Cuba. The crisis could still have escaped political control through local action, accident, or misinterpretation.

The settlement emerged through both public and private channels. Khrushchev accepted removal of the Soviet missiles in exchange for a public pledge that the United States would not invade Cuba. Robert Kennedy also conveyed privately that the United States intended to remove its obsolete Jupiter missiles from Turkey, while insisting this could not appear as a public trade. The Soviet missiles were dismantled; the quarantine continued until remaining issues, including IL-28 bombers, were resolved.

The result was good, but the result is not the answer key. Quarantine was not safe. It left the threat in place during days of intense military readiness and depended on the adversary retaining enough control to bargain. The quality of the decision lies in what it did before the outcome was known: it imposed a cost, communicated a boundary, gathered information, and preserved a ladder of further action.

Post-crisis evidence sharpens the lesson without changing the T0 test. U.S. leaders did not know the location and readiness of all Soviet nuclear warheads in Cuba. An invasion might therefore have encountered nuclear use much earlier than planners expected. That hidden fact explains how much danger was avoided. It should be revealed only after the player decides, because it was not fairly available to Kennedy's team at the moment represented by the case.

PLAYER_FAIRNESS.rationale: Both options receive material advantages and risks using information documented in ExComm records; post-crisis tactical nuclear evidence remains hidden until reveal.

DILEMMA_BALANCE.rationale: Air strike offers speed and removal; quarantine offers reversibility and time. Neither dominates at T0.

CONTEXT_COMPRESSION.rationale: The two-card choice compresses a broader option set but preserves the central strike-versus-quarantine decision documented by the JFK Library.

REVEAL_PAYOFF.rationale: The public/private settlement and unknown Soviet tactical nuclear capability materially deepen the reveal without redefining the player's information.
